newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr rally jeopardised by new rate risk.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr rally jeopardised by new rate risk.

text.p: The Australian dollar was stripped of 1/2 cent of gains and its recovery put in jeopardy Thursday after dire jobs data resurrected talk of a rate cut.

The issue had been thought dead and buried but the market was forced to reconsider when employment showed a shock 33,900 fall against forecasts of a 13,500 rise. The drop pointed to slack in the economy and, as the greatest loss was in the better paid full-time sector, suggested consumers would stay cautious.
"The data are negative for the dollar," said UBS economist Stephen Roberts. "The RBA might conclude there's relatively little risk in trying to underpin faster economic growth."
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local dollar had recoiled to US$0.7800/05 from US$0.7854/59 just before the data hit dealing screens, to be back below Wednesday's late US$0.7810/15.

It had reached as high as US$0.7860 overnight as offshore buying snapped US$0.7820 resistance and caught many short. The tide turned sharply in the wake of the data, however, and many buyers were forced to abandon positions as the day wore on.

Traders said some support had emerged at 78 cents but judged the balance of risks had shifted against it now the data had focused offshore minds on the prospect of narrowing A$ yield differentials, particularly as the U.S. was in tightening mode.
If that proved the case, many saw scope for a correction to US$0.7785 support and could not rule out a return to Tuesday's six-week low of US$0.7735.
The reaction was similar on the crosses, although the dollar remained relatively strong compared to beleagured low yielders like the yen and mark.

The pullback was further fuelled by Japan's Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka who warned the yen's fall was excessive and he would deal decisively with such movements. The U.S. dollar slid over 1/2 yen in response and the local currency followed to 98.05/15 yen from an early 99.62/72 and 99.08/18 late Wednesday.
In trade weighted terms it finished unchanged at 60.6 after reaching as high as 60.9 this morning.

A saving grace in the March jobs data was that unemployment ticked down to 8.7 percent from 8.8 as fewer people went looking for work. Analysts also noted jobs figures were a lagging indicator on the economy and forward looking data pointed to a steady, if slow, pick-up later in the year.

Other sectors of the economy were showing clear signs of recovery, noteably the housing and consumer sectors, and the RBA could feel the effects of its last two cuts in November and December had yet to be felt in full, they said.
However, Roberts at UBS said it was quite possible to build a scenario where an easing looked reasonable.

"The employment weakness, if combined with low inflation indicators in coming weeks, and that includes a relatively low Living Wage claim...would be likely to place discussion of a cut on the agenda at the May 6 RBA board meeting," he said.
This was an untimely prospect for dollar bulls given that the Federal Reserve had just raised U.S. rates and could well tighten again at its May 20 meeting.
The gap between official domestic and U.S. rates was already down to historical lows and even threatened to turn negative.

Indeed, the spread on one-year bonds had already turned tail with the Aussie issue 5.92 percent against 5.96 percent for the comparable Treasury bond. The gap on 10-year bonds had also narrowed to 106 basis points from around 130 last week.
Analysts did add in the dollar's defence that with Australian inflation set to remain around a percentage point below that in the U.S. for this this year, real yield spreads still favoured the A$.
This would tend to underpin it against the yen and European currencies even if it lost ground to the U.S. dollar.
